summary: TechCrunch reports on the Biden administration's long-awaited executive order on AI, announced ahead of an international AI safety summit in the U.K. Experts and stakeholders praised its breadth but stressed that a president cannot do much without legislation, so the order mostly props up voluntary practices and issues guidance. Commenters including Sen. Mark Warner, Paul Barrett, Sheila Gulati and Bob Cattanach called for more legislative action and questioned the timing relative to Vice President Harris's summit remarks.
one_line: Biden's AI executive order drew praise for its breadth, but experts say limited presidential power means real AI regulation needs Congress to act.
key_facts: The Biden administration announced details of its long-awaited AI executive order ahead of an international summit on AI safety in the U.K.
The EO acts as a stopgap that props up the 'voluntary' practices many companies already follow, focusing on sharing results, developing best practices and providing clear guidance.
There is no legislative remedy to AI risks and abuses beyond laws applicable to tech companies in general, which many argue are inadequate.
The EO instructs several AI-focused groups, such as one in the Department of Health and Human Services dedicated to handling and assessing reports of AI-related harms in healthcare.
Senator Mark Warner of Virginia said he was 'impressed by the breadth' of the order but that many sections 'just scratch the surface,' particularly in health care and competition policy.
Paul Barrett, deputy director of the NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights, said the order is 'just the beginning of a regulatory process that will be long and arduous.'

Barrett argued companies profiting from AI should have to prove their products are safe and effective, like makers of pharmaceuticals, industrial chemicals or airplanes, and that the government may lack resources without fresh funding from Congress.

Sheila Gulati, co-founder of Tola Capital, said the EO shows a 'clear intention to walk the line of promoting innovation while protecting citizens' and expects standards bodies, via NIST, to lead over legislators in the near term.
The article notes the federal government is a major customer of AI and tech products, so companies wanting to keep it as a customer will likely follow the EO's lines.
Bob Cattanach, partner at Dorsey and Whitney, said the EO 'awkwardly preempts the voice of Vice President Harris' at the U.K.-hosted AI summit, risking alienating allies by acting unilaterally.
The author notes the U.K. is not the EU and that the EU's 'more collaborative process' will likely take a few more years.
Vice President Harris's remarks at the summit will be streamed on November 1.
The author says it would be a miracle if any substantive AI law passed soon given the state of the legislature and an upcoming contentious election period.
